land.text: their territory 'annexed' with the suppression of the Pannonian revolts of 11-8 BC, then divided among several provinces; 'the territory they dominated covered much of what later became Moesia Superior'

successors.note: In Pannonia one Syrmian community formed the civitas Scordiscorum.

capitals.name: Singidunum (Belgrade)
capitals.note: 'at whose confluence [of the Sava and the Danube] stood their principal settlement, Singidunum'. Taurunum (Zemun) was another Celtic oppidum; the page does not call it a capital. Coordinates are Belgrade's.

correction.text: the Greater Scordisci's core 'between the Sava and the Danube' at Singidunum, with 'the Great Morava valley to some way above Niš, with the routes leading into Macedonia and Thrace'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Scordisci; checked with the gazetteer on 2026-10-19, it draws Serbia only as 1-2 cells of Antigonid Macedonia (270, 200), 1 cell of the Roman Republic (120, 50) and the Roman Empire from about 10 BC (228 cells). The page gives no area; the shape is an 80 km disc round Belgrade plus a 25 km band along the Great Morava (the gazetteer's river), a placeholder for the early core. The page does not date the stages of growth; 'In the 2nd century BC the area under their control reached its greatest extent' is the only dated one.

correction.text: 'much of the territory of modern Serbia and some adjacent lands', 'the lower courses of the main tributaries of the Sava, the Bosna and the Drina', with power 'as far as Paeonia, Illyria and Thrace' (Strabo)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the 2nd-century extent, held to the annexation. Serbia is 71,600 km2 in the gazetteer; the Drina band stands for the lower Bosna and Drina. The Lesser Scordisci 'downstream on both banks of the Danube' (Lower Moesia) and the raids into Macedonia are not drawn as land. The Serbian outline is an approximation (the pages give no frontier); Burebista, whose allies they were around 50 BC, later subdued them (no date on the page), with no loss of land recorded. [Reviewer eu-02-x, 2026-10-19: 'to' -9 to -8 so the last shape reaches the annexation year (end -8)]

region.text: the Sava-Danube confluence at Singidunum and the Great Morava valley

ledger.note: c. 279/278: the Scordisci settle at the Sava-Danube confluence. They 'settled at the confluence of the Sava and the Danube under a leader named Bathanatus' after the Delphi campaign, 'settling there about 279/278 BC and taking the name Scordisci'.

region.text: much of modern Serbia and adjacent lands, up to the lower Bosna and Drina

ledger.note: 2nd century BC: the Scordisci reach their greatest extent. 'In the 2nd century BC the area under their control reached its greatest extent' and 'In the 2nd century BC they were the dominant military power in the region'; the page gives no year, so 200 stands for the century.

region.text: the Scordisci's territory as allies of Rome

ledger.note: 14: Tiberius's punitive campaign (page, paraphrased): in 14 BC Tiberius led a punitive campaign against them, after which they appear only as allies of Rome; the last Scordiscan raid on Macedonia is 16 BC. The clientship is the researcher's reading of 'allies'.
8: the client relation ends in annexation, 'With the suppression of the Pannonian revolts of 11-8 BC their territory was annexed'.

region.text: the Scordisci's territory, now Roman provinces

ledger.note: 8: Rome annexes the Scordisci. 'With the suppression of the Pannonian revolts of 11-8 BC their territory was annexed' and divided among several provinces (Moesia Superior and Pannonia).

wars.name: Roman campaign against the Dalmatians and the Scordisci
wars.outcome: 'In 156 BC the consuls Lucius Lentulus and Gaius Marcius defeated the Dalmatians and the Scordisci'; no land changed hands on the page.
wars.note: The Scordisci 'had fought as allies of the Pannonians'.

wars.name: Scordisci raids on Roman Macedonia
wars.outcome: From about 120 BC 'frequent raids into the province of Macedonia'; they killed the praetor Sextus Pompeius in 119, beat Romans in 141, were beaten by Marcus Annius (119), Minucius Rufus (110-109) and Scipio Asiaticus (84); the last raid recorded is 16 BC (with the Dentheletae); no border moved.
wars.note: Sulla listed them among the peoples brought under Roman authority in 85 BC (page), which is not treated as a loss of land. [Reviewer eu-02-x, 2026-10-19: 'from' -120 to -141: the outcome cites 'In 141 BC the Scordisci defeated the Romans on their own account' (Scordisci page)]

wars.name: Roman conquest of the Scordisci
wars.outcome: Tiberius's punitive campaign of 14 BC left them allies of Rome; the Pannonian revolts of 11-8 BC ended with the territory annexed.

certainty.note: The page names rivers and neighbours (the Taurisci to the north-west, Illyrian mountain peoples to the south) but no frontier; the page calls the society 'heterarchical ... without marked hierarchy or central authority', so the drawn shape is a loose tribal territory.

sources.title: Scordisci
sources.note: Settlement c. 279/278 at the Sava-Danube confluence; territory (Serbia, Great Morava, Bosna and Drina); 2nd-century maximum; wars with Rome 156-14 BC; annexation 11-8 BC. Opened twice (dated sentences, then territory).

notes: One page, because it dates the state's whole life; the dossier is thin on land. The Scordisci are a Celtic tribal people whose page calls them 'heterarchical ... without marked hierarchy or central authority', so 'state' is the project's convention for a polity with a map shape, not the page's word. Start 279 is the Delphi campaign's year ('about 279/278'). The extents are the researcher's: an 80 km disc plus the Great Morava band for the early core (no page dates early growth), Serbia plus a Drina band for the 2nd-century maximum, held to the annexation (the page gives no later loss; Burebista, whose allies they were around 50 BC, later subdued them (undated), Sulla's 85 BC claim of Roman authority is not treated as a change of owner). The Lesser Scordisci downstream on the Danube are not drawn. Gazetteer: all names resolve (Belgrade, Great Morava river, Drina river, Serbia). Counterparts: roman-empire starts 31 BC in Cliopatria, so the 14 and 8 BC events name it; nothing in macedonian/antigonid dossiers records Scordiscan raids as land.
